narrative:
The model estimates that you have a 13% chance of failing your final year—about 13 in every 100 students with a similar pattern would not pass. Although that is a relatively low risk, it is the signal used here to require remedial courses, so the aim is to reduce that risk before the year ends.

The strongest influence on this prediction was your history of past class failures. You have none, which is a clear protective factor and pushed the prediction toward passing. The second strongest was your intention to continue to higher education; wanting to go further in education also worked in your favor. The third factor was your father’s education, which is primary school. This was the main factor pushing toward failing: among students who passed, only about one in seven had a father with primary education, so the model treated this as an added risk.

What matters next is building on the strengths already present. Keep your attendance at zero and protect your current study routine; if possible, increase study time beyond two to five hours a week. Because you are not currently receiving family educational support, ask a parent or guardian for regular help or check-ins. Use your internet access and your goal of higher education as motivation, and speak with a teacher early about a remedial plan so the 13% risk does not grow.
